To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) chronic ethanol consumption in a nonhuman primate model is associated with broad transcriptional changes, including changes in the expression of genes involved in membrane and synapse function and in splicing; and (2) chronic ethanol self‐ administration is also associated with changes in the coexpression and cophenotype (co‐splicing) networks, including changes in hubs and modules.

chronic ethanol self‐consumption by rhesus macaque is associated with widespread gene expression and exon inclusion changes in the brain that are region‐specific and that involve membrane and synaptic genes.
excessive ethanol self-administration in rhesus monkeys was associated with broad expression changes and splicing alterations in the central amygdala and cortical Area 33.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationships between ethanol self‐administration in a non‐humane primate model and the brain transcriptomes of the amygdalar central nucleus and cortical Area 33.
the molecular mechanisms underlying chronic ethanol self‐consumption in a non‐humans primate, and it represents a significant step toward understanding the neurobiology of alcoholism in humans.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of ethanol self‐administration on the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain regions of the animals that self‐administer ethanol show a distinct transcriptional response, with some common and some distinct mechanisms.

excessive ethanol self-administration is associated with broad gene expression and splicing changes, and that these changes include membrane and synaptic genes, but that the specific genes involved are distinct between brain regions and between network types.
chronic ethanol consumption in non‐human primates is a multifaceted phenomenon that is likely to involve a complex set of mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic excessive ethanol self‐administering is associated with widespread changes in gene expression and splicing in two key regions of the brain.
chronic excessive ethanol intake in rhesus monkeys leads to widespread alterations in brain gene transcription that involve both expression and splicing.

excessive ethanol consumption is associated with a large number of transcription and splicing mechanisms in the brain that are largely distinct between brain areas and between expression and cosplicing, and these mechanisms include a number of membrane and synapse‐related gene sets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transcriptomic effects of chronic alcohol intake on the CeA and cortical Area 31 are largely distinct, suggesting that these brain regions are not equally affected by chronic alcohol intake.
excessive self‐administration of ethanol in rhesus monkeys is associated with widespread transcription and splicing mechanisms, including membrane and synapse‐related genes.

the brain transcriptome responds to ethanol self‐administration with complex and diverse transcriptional mechanisms that are region‐specific, and involve distinct sets of genes, gene functions and network types.
